title: Design a Rate Limiter
subtitle: Design distributed enforcement with explicit accuracy, latency, and failure policies
objectives: Turn 'rate limit our API' into a specification with numbers and a failure policy
Design the shared bucket store when the limiter itself must handle your full request volume
Make the check atomic, and decide what happens when the limiter is down
Distribute limits across regions and reason about what exactness really costs

exercises.title: A rate-limit specification defines identity, budget, enforcement, and failure policy
exercises.body: Specify the key being limited, budget and time window, permitted burst, response on breach, required enforcement accuracy, and behavior when counter storage fails. These inputs determine the algorithm, state placement, and whether requests need shared coordination.
exercises.note: An undocumented fail-open or fail-closed choice turns a counter-store outage into either uncontrolled traffic or a full API outage.

exercises.prompt: Three API servers each enforce 100 req/min in local memory, so one client can send 300. Move the counter to one shared atomic store.
exercises.beforeStatus: EFFECTIVE CLIENT LIMIT · 300 req/min across three servers
exercises.afterStatus: EFFECTIVE CLIENT LIMIT · 100 req/min across the fleet
exercises.result: The fleet began enforcing one limit
exercises.why: An atomic shared counter gives every server the same view of the client's usage, so the limit applies across the fleet. It adds a network operation to the request path and the counter store must handle the resulting traffic.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Three API servers each enforce 100 req/min in local memory, so one client can send 300. Move the counter to one shared atomic store. Place API fleet, Shared counter. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client → API fleet; API fleet → Shared counter. That topology is the evidence for the answer: An atomic shared counter gives every server the same view of the client's usage, so the limit applies across the fleet. It adds a network operation to the request path and the counter store must handle the resulting traffic.

exercises.prompt: 'Build a rate limiter for our API.' What must you pin down before designing anything?
choices: What's being limited (the key), the limit and window, what happens on breach, and how exact it has to be
exercises.why: Identity, resource scope, time window, and required precision determine the counter key and enforcement mechanism. Exact global limits require more coordination than approximate local limits, so the acceptable overshoot must be specified before choosing storage and topology.

exercises.prompt: What makes a rate limiter unusual compared to every system so far?
choices: It sits in front of everything, so it sees 100% of traffic and must be faster and more available than the service it protects — if it's slow, everything is slow
exercises.why: A front-door limiter evaluates every request before downstream work. Its latency is added to every request, and a fail-closed outage can reject all traffic, so it needs high availability and an explicit behavior when its state store is unavailable.

exercises.prompt: Your API handles 500,000 requests/second. How many rate limit checks per second must the limiter perform?
exercises.why: At 500,000 incoming requests/sec, exact enforcement performs 500,000 counter decisions/sec because checks cannot be sampled without missing violations. This rate must be distributed, batched, or filtered locally if one shared store cannot sustain the operations and network round trips.

exercises.prompt: Each check is a read and a write to a counter. Why can't you just add read replicas?
choices: Because the check-and-increment must see the current value: reading a lagging replica means two servers both see 99 and both allow — replication scales reads, and this is a write
exercises.why: An exact limiter updates shared state for each accepted request, and a stale replica can admit traffic after the authoritative count has reached the limit. Read replicas therefore do not remove the authoritative update bottleneck; independent counter keys can be sharded, or enforcement can accept bounded approximation.

exercises.prompt: What should happen when a request is rejected?
choices: Return 429 with `Retry-After`, plus headers showing the limit, what's remaining, and when it resets — so clients can self-regulate instead of discovering the limit by hitting it
Queue it until capacity frees up
exercises.why: `429 Too Many Requests` identifies a limit breach, while quota and `Retry-After` headers let cooperative clients reduce or schedule future requests. Queueing over-limit requests retains connections and memory and delays work the system has already decided it cannot serve.

exercises.prompt: Spec so far: token bucket, 1,000 requests/minute per API key, 429 on breach. What's still missing?
choices: The failure policy: when the bucket store is unreachable, do you allow everything or block everything? That decision exists whether or not you make it
exercises.why: When the bucket store is unavailable, fail-open preserves API availability but may admit abusive load, while fail-closed preserves the limit but can turn a limiter failure into an API outage. The specification must choose based on the harm the limit is intended to prevent.

exercises.title: A shared token bucket refills and consumes atomically per limit key
exercises.body: Store `tokens` and `last_refill_time` for each client key. One atomic operation computes refill from elapsed time, caps tokens at bucket capacity, and consumes one token only when available. All API servers call that same logical bucket.
exercises.note: Hash-sharding distributes independent keys, but one extremely hot key still concentrates all of its atomic operations on one shard.

exercises.prompt: Your limiter runs on 50 API servers, each keeping counters in local memory. What's the actual limit a client experiences?
choices: Up to 50× it, because each server counts only what it saw — you configured 1,000 and shipped 50,000
exercises.why: Each of 50 servers independently permits up to 1,000 requests because none sees the others' counters. A client distributed across the fleet can therefore receive up to 50,000 requests per window unless the budget is divided or the state is shared.

exercises.prompt: You need one shared token bucket per API key across all 50 servers. Add the piece.
exercises.why: A shared bucket makes every API server observe the same tokens and refill timestamp before admission. A fast key-value store can run the single-key check-and-consume atomically; stale replica reads or asynchronous queue processing cannot enforce the boundary at request time.

exercises.prompt: Your token-bucket code reads tokens and the last-refill time, computes a refill, then writes the result. What's the bug?
choices: Reading two fields is too slow
It's check-then-act: concurrent requests can both observe the same token and both consume it
Tokens must be stored in every API server
exercises.why: Concurrent requests can read the same token balance and refill timestamp before either writes, so both may spend one remaining token. Refill calculation, capacity capping, admission, and conditional consumption must be one serialized operation for that key.

exercises.prompt: So what must one atomic server-side token-bucket operation do?
choices: Increment a fixed-window counter, even for rejected requests
Load tokens and refill time, add elapsed-time refill up to capacity, consume only if a token exists, then save and return the decision
Read from a replica, then update the leader later
Reset the bucket whenever a request is rejected
exercises.why: A script or equivalent single-key transaction uses elapsed time to refill continuously, caps the balance at burst capacity, and decrements only an allowed request. Rejected traffic therefore cannot drive the balance below zero or extend denial, and concurrent requests cannot spend the same token. Expiry is optional cleanup after the bucket has remained full and idle, not the limiter's refill mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Peak load is 500,000 checks/sec. One bucket shard safely handles 100,000 checks/sec. Build a six-shard limiter: five shards cover peak load and one provides headroom. Each API key must map to one primary shard before the gateway sends an allowed request to the backend.

nodes.sub: map API key to one primary

exercises.why: Five shards provide the stated 500,000-check peak capacity and the sixth adds 20% headroom. The router deterministically maps one API key to one primary shard, which atomically refills and consumes that key's bucket. The bucket cluster returns an allow/deny decision to the gateway; it does not forward the application request. Only after `ALLOW` does the gateway call the backend. Consistent hashing is optional when membership changes frequently, not a requirement for ordinary deterministic partitioning.

exercises.prompt: A single enormous customer sends 200,000 requests/second by themselves. What breaks?
choices: Their bucket is one key on one shard, so that shard takes 200,000 ops/sec — the celebrity problem, and key sharding cannot split one hot bucket
exercises.why: Key-based sharding keeps one customer's bucket on one node, so a 200,000 requests/sec customer can overload that shard. Splitting the customer's budget into leased sub-buckets spreads operations, but lease size and rebalancing determine the bound on temporary underuse or overshoot.

exercises.title: Exact shared enforcement adds a counter-store dependency to every request
exercises.body: Before admitting a request, the gateway sends an atomic check-and-update to shared storage and waits for the result. This adds one store round trip to allowed and rejected traffic, and the store's latency and availability become part of the API's critical path.
exercises.note: A globally exact budget adds cross-region coordination; partitioning budget among regions reduces latency while allowing bounded enforcement error.

exercises.prompt: Every check is a Redis round trip — say 0.5ms. What have you added to every single API request?
choices: 0.5ms of latency and a hard dependency, on 100% of requests — including the ones you were going to serve anyway
exercises.why: A synchronous 0.5 ms counter round trip adds approximately 0.5 ms to every request on the serial path, including requests far below the limit. That latency and store load are justified only when the cost of limit error requires exact shared enforcement.

exercises.prompt: So how do you get most of the protection without paying that hop on every request?
choices: Check a local counter first: an obvious flood is rejected instantly with no network call, and only borderline traffic goes to the shared store for exact accounting
exercises.why: A local approximate limiter can reject traffic that is far above the threshold without consulting shared state. Requests near the boundary continue to the exact shared check, reducing round trips while preserving precision where the decision could change.

exercises.prompt: A contractual spend cap says this customer must never exceed 100,000 admitted requests/day. Slide toward your enforcement design.
exercises.why: A hard contractual cap makes over-admission a correctness failure, so the admission path needs an exact coordinated quota or preallocated sub-budgets whose total never exceeds 100,000. Billing still needs a separate durable usage ledger: an ephemeral limiter can protect a boundary, but it is not authoritative financial metering.

exercises.prompt: Redis goes down. Your limiter can't check anything. What should happen?
choices: It depends on what the limit protects: fail open if it guards against noisy neighbours, fail closed if it guards something that costs money or can be abused
exercises.why: For a courtesy limit, fail-open may preserve the more important service availability. For an abuse boundary or a limit protecting a costly resource, fail-closed may prevent unacceptable load or spend; repeated synchronous retries add latency and load while postponing the same policy decision.

exercises.prompt: You run in three regions. A client's limit is 1,000/minute globally. Should the counter be global?
choices: Yes — the limit is global, so the counter must be
Usually not: fixed regional shares keep checks local and never exceed the allocated total, but skewed traffic can strand unused capacity
No — limits should be per-region by policy
exercises.why: A single exact global bucket adds cross-region coordination to each request. Fixed shares such as 400, 300, and 300 requests/minute sum to exactly 1,000, so they cannot overshoot but can reject in a busy region while another region has unused tokens. Borrowing or delayed reconciliation improves utilization only by introducing a quantified overshoot risk or coordination step.

exercises.prompt: Traffic is uneven across three regions. Which regional design honestly describes its tradeoff?
choices: Three fixed shares overshoot the global allocation whenever traffic is uneven
Fixed shares preserve the 1,000 total but may underuse it; independent full allowances can overshoot by up to 2,000; borrowing needs a stated bound
Delayed reconciliation makes a limit exact at request time
Any regional design behaves like one global atomic bucket
exercises.why: If three fixed shares sum to 1,000, aggregate admissions cannot exceed 1,000, but a hot region can reject while tokens sit idle elsewhere. Giving every region the full 1,000 can admit 3,000 before reconciliation, an overshoot of 2,000. Leasing or borrowing can trade between those outcomes only with an explicit lease size, coordination rule, and published bound.

exercises.title: Cost-weighted limits charge requests in resource units
exercises.body: Assign each operation a token weight based on expected CPU, database, bandwidth, or external-service cost. Admission subtracts that weight from the caller's budget, so an expensive report consumes more capacity than a cached lookup even though both are one HTTP request.
exercises.note: If actual cost is unknown before execution, reserve an estimate during admission and reconcile the difference after completion.

exercises.prompt: A single image export consumes about as much compute as 20 profile reads, but both currently cost one token. Protect capacity using work-based prices.
exercises.beforeStatus: LIMIT · export = 1 token · profile read = 1 token
exercises.afterStatus: LIMIT · export = 20 tokens · profile read = 1 token
exercises.result: Expensive operations now consume proportionate capacity from the budget
exercises.why: Request counts protect capacity only when requests have similar cost. Weighted tokens approximate CPU, database, or downstream work. Measure real resource use and revise weights as implementations change.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A single image export consumes about as much compute as 20 profile reads, but both currently cost one token. Protect capacity using work-based prices. Place Weighted bucket. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Image export → Weighted bucket; Profile read → Weighted bucket. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Request counts protect capacity only when requests have similar cost. Weighted tokens approximate CPU, database, or downstream work. Measure real resource use and revise weights as implementations change.

exercises.prompt: Your limiter counts requests. One endpoint runs a 30-second report; another returns a cached string. What's wrong?
choices: Nothing — a request is a request
A request count is a proxy for load, and it stops describing anything once requests differ by 15,000× in cost — a client burning your fleet looks identical to one fetching cached strings
The report endpoint needs its own service
The cached endpoint shouldn't be limited
exercises.why: One report request can consume much more CPU or database time than one cached lookup, so equal request counts do not represent equal resource use. Weighted tokens charge expensive endpoints more and align the enforced budget with the constrained resource.

exercises.prompt: Your limiter is the front door for everything. Which properties does it need? Select all.
choices: Higher availability than the services behind it
Latency low enough to be invisible in the request path
A defined behaviour when its own dependencies fail
exercises.why: Because the limiter is on the critical path, it needs low latency, high availability, and a defined store-failure policy. Window counters are derived and expire quickly, so durable recovery is often less important than continued enforcement or a controlled fail-open behavior.

exercises.prompt: Where should the limiter run?
choices: At the edge or gateway, before you've spent anything — the value of a rejection is proportional to how little it cost you
exercises.why: Rejecting at an edge gateway avoids body parsing and downstream application or database work. If the limit key depends on identity, the gateway must perform enough inexpensive authentication to derive that identity before applying the counter.

exercises.prompt: 10,000 clients get limited at once and all obey `Retry-After`: 60. What have you built?
choices: A synchronized stampede: every client returns at the same instant because you told them all the same number — obedience produced the spike
exercises.why: An identical `Retry-After: 60` aligns 10,000 clients on the same retry instant, creating another traffic spike. Adding random jitter to the delay spreads attempts across an interval while still communicating when capacity is expected to return.

exercises.prompt: A single client's limit is enforced correctly — but 10,000 clients each at their limit still overwhelm you. What's missing?
choices: Per-client limits sum to no bound at all: you also need a global load-shedding layer that protects total capacity regardless of who's asking
exercises.why: A per-client limit enforces fairness independently, so the sum of many compliant clients can still exceed fleet capacity. A separate global concurrency or traffic limit sheds aggregate load when the service is saturated, regardless of which clients generated it.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the rate limiter design.
choices: A counter in Redis with a TTL
An atomic token-bucket check on sharded shared state, run before backend work — with deliberate failure, regional-budget, hotspot, and overload policies
exercises.why: A distributed token bucket stores tokens and refill time per limit key and updates them atomically before admitting work. Key sharding distributes customers, while regional budgets, hot-key handling, cost-weighted tokens, overload shedding, and fail-open or fail-closed behavior define the tradeoffs among precision, latency, availability, and backend protection.

exercises.title: The limiter is a control-plane decision on the request path, not a proxy for backend work
exercises.body: The gateway derives a policy key such as tenant, API key, endpoint class, and region. Consistent routing sends that key to one authoritative bucket shard, which atomically refills and consumes tokens. An allow decision returns to the gateway; the gateway—not the bucket store—continues the request to the backend.
exercises.note: Sharding aggregate checks does not split one hot key. A tenant that exceeds one shard's capacity needs hierarchical limits, admission before expensive parsing, or an explicitly partitionable policy.

exercises.prompt: Every request waits on a global counter store in Virginia. European API latency gains 90ms, even though limits permit bounded regional overshoot.
choices: Keep the global hop for every request
Lease bounded token budgets to regional limiters and reconcile usage
choiceFeedback: The design preserves exactness but violates the accepted latency tradeoff.
Regional leases bound total overshoot while moving ordinary decisions near traffic.
Disabling enforcement creates unbounded exposure rather than a stated tradeoff.
exercises.beforeStatus: EU REQUEST · +90ms global counter round trip
exercises.afterStatus: EU REQUEST · local atomic consume · bounded leased budget
exercises.result: Latency improves while overshoot remains explicitly bounded
exercises.why: When the requirement permits bounded inaccuracy, leasing partitions the global budget rather than pretending independent regional limits remain global. Lease size controls the maximum unused or overspent capacity during delay and partition.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Every request waits on a global counter store in Virginia. European API latency gains 90ms, even though limits permit bounded regional overshoot. Place EU limiter, US limiter. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Global allocator → EU limiter; Global allocator → US limiter. That topology is the evidence for the answer: When the requirement permits bounded inaccuracy, leasing partitions the global budget rather than pretending independent regional limits remain global. Lease size controls the maximum unused or overspent capacity during delay and partition.

exercises.prompt: Match each limiter record field to the decision it supports.

pairs.right: Identifies the principal and policy bucket being charged
Computes elapsed replenishment inside the atomic operation
Prevents stale configuration from silently applying the wrong budget

exercises.why: An atomic bucket operation needs identity, balance, and elapsed-time state. Versioning connects runtime counters to the policy that created them, which matters during gradual configuration rollout and rollback.

exercises.prompt: A design review finds per-server counters, read-then-write token updates, one token for every endpoint, and immediate retries after `429`. Which failures follow? Select all.
choices: Clients multiply their limit by the server count
Concurrent checks overspend the same tokens
Rejected clients can synchronize into another traffic spike
exercises.why: Each defect violates a different part of enforcement: shared identity, atomic consumption, cost modelling, and retry behavior. A rate limiter protects capacity only when the whole request path and client response are designed together.

exercises.prompt: Build the allowed-request path: one gateway derives the key, one bucket shard decides, and backend work starts only after allow.
exercises.why: The gateway sends a small decision request to the one shard responsible for the key. An allow result returns to the gateway, which then invokes the backend. The bucket store is authoritative for admission state but never carries application traffic.

exercises.prompt: An AI endpoint allows 100 requests/minute, but one request costs 1 token and another costs 100,000. What should admission consume?
choices: Cost-weighted tokens based on protected work
Exactly one token per HTTP request
exercises.why: Request count is not a useful capacity proxy when work varies by five orders of magnitude. Weighted tokens align admission with the constrained compute or spend budget.
